definition: A range computed so that, over many repeated samples, about 95% of such ranges would contain the true value.
A 95% interval for a rate, such as a comeback rate. Unlike the simplest formula, it stays reliable when a rate is near zero or a sample is small. Its two ends are the Wilson bounds.
A 95% interval for the difference between two rates, built from each rate's Wilson interval.
A correction for making many comparisons at once. Each interval is widened so that the chance of any false alarm across all the comparisons stays near 5%.
Hal Stern's 1994 model of a game's score margin. It treats the margin as a random walk, so it needs only the lead, the time left, and sigma to give a win chance.
A path in which each step is random and does not depend on earlier steps.
The model's measure of volatility, in points per square root of a minute. The margin's typical swing over T minutes is sigma times the square root of T.
A steady tilt of the margin toward one team. With no drift, the model treats the margin as equally likely to move either way from here.

The smallest lead at which that lead and every larger one are lost no more than a set share of the time. The 1% safe lead uses 1%. The model's version is the lead where its win chance for the trailing team falls to 1%.
Adjusted so that a bigger lead never shows a higher comeback rate than a smaller one. The method, pool-adjacent-violators, averages neighboring rates that break this order, weighted by games.
The plain difference between two percentages. A move from 5% to 7% is 2 percentage points.
A fixed moment in a game when the study reads who leads and by how much.
The league's event-by-event log of a game, including the running score.
